label: map_1
name: Rule-Rendered Shorthand Decoder
mech: Task: historical shorthand archives, which AI has avoided because meaning is carried by stroke weight, slant and line position, and there is almost no labeled data. A procedural renderer encodes each shorthand system's rulebook and turns modern text into synthetic pages with jittered, pen-pressure strokes. These synthetic pages train a 25M-parameter stroke-vectorizing CNN encoder. That encoder feeds a differentiable finite-state transducer, built from the same rulebook, which outputs a phonetic lattice. A 100M-parameter language model of the target era rescores the lattice. The model then self-trains on unlabeled scans by keeping only high-confidence lattice paths. All models are small and the FST is sparse, so training fits in 12 GB of VRAM and synthetic data costs nothing to generate.
value: It can read a writing system that has no training corpus, because the shorthand rules themselves supply the labels.

label: map_1
name: Notation-to-Physics Choreography Engine
mech: Task: Labanotation dance scores, which motion AI has ignored because no paired score-and-motion data exists. A rule-based notator converts public motion-capture data (for example AMASS) into Labanotation symbol columns, which creates millions of synthetic pairs. A symbol-graph transformer (about 60M parameters) reads each column's symbols, durations and body-part staff. It outputs target poses and timing for a physics-simulated skeleton, run as a GPU rigid-body simulation at 24 joints. Training combines pose-reconstruction loss, a loss for re-notating the generated motion and matching the score, and balance and torque penalties. Then the model is fine-tuned on a few dozen real scores that have archival film.
value: Archival scores become physically plausible performances that a dancer can watch and learn from.

label: map_1
name: Single-Board Warp Forecaster
mech: Task: forecasting how one specific plank will move. AI has been absent because wood science works at species level and grading AI needs industrial scanners. Phone photos of both end-grain faces and two long faces feed a 30M-parameter U-Net. It infers a 3D field of growth-ring orientation, density and sapwood/heartwood. That field drives a differentiable finite-element model with about 20k elements, using orthotropic shrinkage, which predicts cup, bow and twist under any humidity schedule. The network pretrains on procedurally grown synthetic logs sawn virtually. It then self-supervises from users photographing the same board at two humidity levels: the measured deformation becomes the loss, backpropagated through the finite-element model. The finite-element model runs in milliseconds on the GPU, and the photo-to-field network is small.
value: Woodworkers can choose and orient individual boards before cutting, which no lumber-grading system or species table can do.

label: map_2
name: Fracture-Physics Lithic Refitting Engine
mech: The task is refitting excavated stone flakes back onto their cores to recover how prehistoric tools were knapped. Archaeologists still do this by hand over years because datasets are tiny, the fragments are plain grey rock, and generic 3D matchers ignore fracture physics. Each flake and core is scanned with a phone into a 20k-point cloud. A 15M-parameter point transformer embeds every fracture surface (scars, bulb, ripple direction), and a neural implicit "fracture field" predicts which flake would break off for any core state and strike. Most training is synthetic: a low-resolution GPU fracture simulator generates millions of (core, strike, flake) triples overnight, and a contrastive loss on the few hundred published refit sets aligns the model to real scans. At inference, a beam search over removal order puts the flakes back onto the core and scores each step for physical plausibility, all within 6 GB of VRAM.
value: It reconstructs the full knapping order from a pile of debris, which shape-matching alone cannot do because neighbouring flakes rarely share clean edges.

label: map_2
name: Ensemble-Aware Gamelan Retuning Model
mech: The task is retuning or replacing keys of a Balinese or Javanese gamelan. Each ensemble has its own tuning (embat) and its own beating between paired instruments (ombak), so no equal-tempered tool applies and AI has never been tried. The inputs are tap recordings of every key plus a phone 3D scan of the damaged or new bronze key. A set transformer over all the keys' measured overtone spectra learns a latent embat vector for the ensemble, and a mesh graph network stands in for finite-element vibration analysis, mapping key shape to its first eight overtones. The output is a grinding map: an optimization through that stand-in model proposes where and how much bronze to remove so the key matches the ensemble's target overtones and its beat rate against its partner. The stand-in model trains on about 200k GPU finite-element simulations of randomized key shapes (hours on a 3060), and the embat encoder trains on a few hundred recorded ensembles by learning to reconstruct masked keys.
value: It lets a non-specialist restore a gamelan's own tuning signature, which a generic tuner cannot even define.

label: map_2
name: Formant-to-Whistle Bridge Transcoder
mech: The task is transcribing and teaching whistled languages (Silbo Gomero, Turkish kuş dili, Hmong whistled speech). They have only minutes to hours of recordings and no written corpus, and speech recognition treats them as music. The model forces everything through an explicit articulatory bottleneck: a distilled 30M-parameter encoder trained on ordinary spoken Spanish or Turkish predicts F2 formant paths and consonant types. A differentiable layer, initialized from linguists' rules, then turns those into a single whistle pitch-and-loudness contour. Training uses cycle consistency (speech to synthetic whistle to recovered phonemes), plus a small adversarial loss against the few real whistle recordings. The reverse decoder outputs phoneme lattices that a small spoken-language model held in system RAM rescores, and the whole system stays under 100M parameters and trains in days with mixed precision.
value: It learns whistled speech from spoken-language data alone, where any end-to-end model fails for lack of transcribed whistle recordings.

label: map_3
name: Inverse Glaze Chemistry Solver
mech: Potters still develop ceramic glazes by firing test tiles one at a time. AI has failed here because the data are small and noisy (about 20k community recipes with uneven photos), and surface color depends nonlinearly on oxide chemistry, kiln atmosphere and cooling, which gives generic vision models nothing to anchor to. The model turns a recipe into oxide ratios (Unity Molecular Formula) through a frozen stoichiometry layer that maps materials to oxides. A 30M-parameter conditional decoder takes those ratios plus cone, atmosphere and cooling curve and predicts calibrated Lab color, gloss and the probabilities of crawling and crazing. It trains on photos white-balanced against a printed color card, and a crazing head is supervised by thermal-expansion mismatch computed against the clay body. At inference, gradient descent in recipe space restricted to the user's own materials finds a recipe for a target photo. Training takes about 6 GPU-hours and a search takes seconds.
value: A potter photographs a surface they want and gets a recipe made from materials they own that is chemically valid and safe from crazing, which neither an image generator nor a recipe lookup can give.

label: map_3
name: Violin Plate Carving Copilot
mech: Luthiers shape spruce violin plates by tapping them and listening for the free-plate modes (1, 2 and 5). AI has stayed out because every billet of wood is different and no datasets exist. A material-identification network reads phone recordings of taps at 5 points plus a few caliper readings. It infers the wood's directional stiffness values and density. A graph-network surrogate on a 2k-node plate mesh predicts mode frequencies and shapes from a thickness map plus those material values. It trains on about 2M finite-element eigen-solves run on the same PC's CPU and 32 GB of RAM (about a week), then is fine-tuned on a few real plates. Carving advice comes from optimizing the surrogate under a remove-wood-only constraint, which outputs a map of how much wood to take off and where to hit the target modes.
value: It predicts the acoustic effect of cuts that cannot be undone before the gouge touches the wood, which no audio app or generic simulator does for a specific plank.

label: map_3
name: Smartphone Tree-Ring Dating
mech: Dating old timber from its tree rings (dendrochronology) needs cores, microscopes and an expert to match ring widths against regional records. Machine learning has only detected rings on clean lab scans and has never dated a rough phone photo of a barn beam or a stump. An 8M-parameter U-Net traces several radial paths and extracts ring-width series with an uncertainty for each ring. An encoder turns the detrended series into embeddings. Dating then treats offset-only matching as a 1D convolution against about 4,000 regional chronologies from the ITRDB public tree-ring database, held in RAM. The result is a probability for each calendar year of the outermost ring, plus species and region. Training uses the database's millions of measured series, rendered into synthetic wood images with saw marks, cracks and missing or false rings, so both stages learn end to end.
value: Homeowners and conservators get a calendar date with a stated confidence from one photo, where today it takes a lab visit and weeks of expert matching.

label: g1_neg
name: Lighting Cues from Edit Logs
mech: Task: programming lighting cues for live theatre. AI has never been used here, and DJ "sound-to-light" fails because it reacts to loudness and ignores the drama. Inputs are the lighting console's channel states (compressed by a small autoencoder that groups channels into about 256 fixture tokens), the script position aligned to rehearsal audio, and the cue history. A 60M-parameter transformer outputs the change to the next cue state and its fade time. It is pretrained on thousands of show files that designers share. It is then fine-tuned on the designer's own edit and undo stream from technical rehearsals, where each correction is a preference pair. Everything fits in 12 GB at FP16, and inference runs live during rehearsal.
value: It learns one designer's personal style in a single technical week and drafts the next 300 cues, which neither a generic model nor reactive sound-to-light can do.

label: g1_neg
name: Kitchen Firing Policy
mech: Task: deciding when each dish on each order is started ("fired") in a small restaurant kitchen. Kitchen display systems use fixed timers, and no learning system has ever modelled how cooking stations compete for time. Inputs are an event stream of open orders (items, modifiers, station), each station's queue, the cooks on shift, and the time. A 20M-parameter transformer that treats the open orders as a set outputs, for each item, a probability of firing it now. It is trained by offline RL (implicit Q-learning) on the timestamp logs already stored in the point-of-sale and display systems. The reward favours a table's courses reaching the pass together, short order times and few remakes. A year of logs is about 1M events, and it trains overnight on the 3060.
value: It times orders across the stations that compete for the same cooks and equipment, using only that restaurant's existing logs, which fixed timers and generic arrival-time predictors cannot do.

label: g1_neg
name: Bridge Partnership Misunderstanding Detector
mech: Task: finding where two particular bridge partners interpret their bids differently. Existing bridge bots model a standard bidding system, not the private habits of a real pair. Inputs are the auction as tokens, the bidder's hand and a learned partnership embedding; per-pair LoRA adapters sit on a 40M-parameter base. Outputs are a posterior over the partner's suit lengths and high-card points, plus the action the partner will take next. Training uses millions of online hand records, where all four hands are revealed after play, so every auction comes with the true hands. When what the partner inferred, judged from their next bid, differs sharply from what the bidder actually held, that agreement is flagged as misunderstood.
value: It points to the exact agreements a specific partnership misreads, which no general bridge bot or coach could find from the same data.

label: g1_core
name: Cave Impedance Plethysmograph
mech: Natural changes in air pressure (barometric tides and weather fronts) serve as the forcing signal, and a cheap ultrasonic anemometer at each entrance records the airflow response. Together they give an impedance spectrum Z(f) per entrance, the same way the forced oscillation technique tests lungs. A small transformer maps the spectrum, plus the volume and resistance already known from the survey, to a posterior over a multi-compartment model (an Otis-style network of resistances and compliances): how many hidden compartments there are, how big they are, and how strongly they are connected. It is trained on millions of synthetic networks made by deleting passages from real surveys, then fine-tuned on caves whose volume was later measured. The model is under 20M parameters and trains in hours on the 3060.
value: It gives a measured, uncertainty-bounded estimate of volume nobody has entered yet from a $40 sensor, where the same budget otherwise buys only geologic guesswork.

label: g1_core
name: Passage Scaffolding From Mate-Evidence
mech: Surveyed passage segments are treated like contigs (assembled genome fragments). "Mate-pair" links between separate passage ends come from dye traces, cave radio fixes, cross-correlated temperature and airflow loggers (the lag gives the travel distance), and shared sediments. A genome-scaffolder engine keeps a graph of passage ends with a distribution of gap lengths on each edge. It solves ordering and orientation with an exact integer program, held in RAM. A graph network, trained on the dated history of club surveys (hide connections found later, then predict them), scores how plausible each edge is from rock-layer orientation and fracture alignment taken from the elevation model. The output is the most likely set of connections with gap lengths, which turns into dig targets.
value: It combines different kinds of weak evidence into connection hypotheses that can be checked, which no geometric interpolation can do.

label: g1_core
name: ETAS Discovery Forecaster
mech: Every dated survey leg is treated as an event in a self-exciting point process, as in aftershock forecasting. A background intensity field comes from a small CNN over the elevation model and geology layers, and each discovery raises the chance of more discoveries nearby, fading over time and distance (Omori-like kernels). Parameters are fitted by maximum likelihood on decades of version-controlled club survey history. The output is the expected new passage per trip for each open lead, which feeds a simple scheduler for expedition planning. The whole model fits in under 1 GB and fits in minutes.
value: It turns the exploration record itself into a calibrated forecast of where effort will pay off, which caver intuition and geology-only maps cannot provide.

label: g1_core2
name: Spark Kalman Vertex Tracker
mech: A tiny convolutional hit detector (~2M parameters) runs on each frame of 240 fps video and outputs streak-segment "hits" with position, direction and two-colour brightness ratio. A bank of Kalman filters follows each spark with a ballistic state (position, velocity, drag coefficient, temperature) and a predict/correct update, as charged-particle tracking does. Vertex finding detects burst points where one track ends and several begin. The detector is trained self-supervised: it is rewarded for hits that Kalman tracks predict with high likelihood, and frames are alternated with track refits (EM). No labels are needed. Everything fits easily in 12 GB and runs at video rate on a 3060.
value: It turns an unlabelled phone clip into a physical event record: drag-derived particle size, colour temperature and burst vertices. Pixel classifiers trained on the same budget cannot produce these quantities, and they break when the camera or lighting changes.

label: g1_core2
name: Phylodynamic Spark Burst Inference
mech: The tracked bursts from Idea 1 form genealogies: carrier line, first fork, second-generation forks. These are scored under a multitype Galton–Watson branching process with timed delays. The process's offspring mean, generation depth and delay distribution are estimated by exact tree likelihood, as phylodynamics estimates R from pathogen trees. Carbon drives CO-explosion branching. Elements such as Mn, Cr, W and Mo shift the delay distribution, the colour type and terminal shapes (W gives dull red; Mo gives detached "arrowhead" tips). Pressure changes how many trees appear, not the statistics within each tree, so the estimates do not depend on it. Inference is CPU-bound over a few thousand trees and runs in seconds in 32 GB RAM.
value: Its composition estimates come from per-tree statistics that stay the same across grinders, wheels and operators, which no same-budget image model can match.

label: g1_core2
name: Mixed-Effects Session Calibration
mech: Following population-pharmacokinetics practice, the branching and track parameters are modelled as composition fixed effects (shared across every user) plus random effects for each session (wheel grit, RPM, camera white balance), with fixed and random effects fitted jointly by Laplace approximation. In each session the user grinds one or two reference bars of known grade, which pin down that session's random effects. Each unknown bar then gets a posterior over a grade list, with credible intervals. Fixed effects are refined as uploaded sessions accumulate, and each new session needs only seconds of CPU on the PC. The posterior feeds a small lookup table of heat treatments (hardening temperature, quench medium, temper) that takes the uncertainty into account.
value: It gives calibrated "this is probably 1080 versus O1, here is how sure" answers, and recommends the right quench for unknown scrap, from two reference bars per session instead of thousands of labelled samples.

label: g1_mech
name: Seasonal Riverbed Reveal
mech: The task is showing paddlers, before they commit, where submerged rocks, undercuts and trapped logs sit under fast whitewater. AI has been absent here because nobody has ground truth for what lies beneath moving water. Input is a 10-second phone clip of a rapid. Tracking how foam patches move from frame to frame gives a 128x128 field of surface speed and direction plus a surface-texture field. A learned function of about 5M weights maps these to a grid of depth below the surface and a per-cell probability that water flows under rock. The seasons supply training pairs for free: the same stretch is filmed at high water and photographed at low water, and the two are aligned by GPS and fixed landmarks, so the riverbed exposed at low flow is the target for the high-flow surface. The weights are driven by the gap between predicted and exposed bed heights, with the gauge-level difference as an extra input. Model and batches fit in 12 GB, a few thousand river-stretch pairs train in days, and a clip is answered in under a second.
value: Paddlers get a read of what the surface hides from a phone, which no same-budget sensor or rule of thumb provides.

label: g1_mech
name: Footprint Decay Clock
mech: The task is estimating how many hours ago a footprint was pressed into mud, sand or snow, so search-and-rescue teams can tell which trail is fresh. AI has failed here because no aged tracks with known times exist, and how a print decays depends on the weather since it was made. Volunteers press a standard boot into the ground next to a staked phone that photographs the print every 20 minutes from two flash angles, while a cheap weather station logs temperature, rain and wind. Each photo pair becomes a relief stored as rim sharpness, wall slope and fill-depth profiles. A small learned function takes the current profiles plus the weather summed since each candidate start time and scores every elapsed-hour bin. Training pushes the true elapsed time to the top score, and an ordering penalty forces later photos of the same print to be judged older. Each print is a few thousand numbers and the weather sums live in RAM, so millions of timed photos train on one GPU.
value: From a single photo it gives a calibrated age range such as "3-6 h ago" with its uncertainty, which trackers' intuition cannot give consistently.

label: g1_mech
name: Neighbour-Predicted Tap Map
mech: The task is finding hidden rot in wooden boat hulls and timber frames, where surveyors tap with a hammer and listen. AI is absent because every hull rings differently, so fixed sound-to-rot rules never carry over from one hull to the next. The user taps about 300 points while the phone films the hammer head to get each position and records each 50 ms ring. Each ring is reduced to a 64-band spectrum plus a decay rate per band. A learned function of under 1M weights predicts each tap's spectrum from its 8 nearest neighbours' spectra, their distances and the grain direction. Sound wood is predictable from its neighbours, so the per-point prediction error forms the rot map. Training first hides points on thousands of hulls and predicts them back. A small second stage then maps error maps to awl-probe softness depths that surveyors record when the boats are hauled out, and both stages train overnight.
value: It gives an objective rot map for each hull from a phone and a hammer, where a generic sound classifier on the same budget fails because no two hulls share a baseline.

label: g1_loop
name: Residual-Tested Stratigraphy Builder
mech: The task is building an archaeological Harris matrix, the ordering of soil layers, from trench photos, level readings and excavators' notes. AI has been absent because each site is unique, labels are tiny and errors are buried in hand-drawn sheets. A 30M-parameter segmentation-plus-relation network turns photos and notes into a graph: nodes are contexts typed deposit, cut or fill, and edges are above/below relations with confidences. A weighted least-squares "state estimator" fits a latent depth-time coordinate to each node from every redundant relation and elevation. The largest normalized residual (power-grid test) names the single worst relation, which is then deleted, reversed, or used to re-type its node. Training is self-supervised from internal consistency on about 200 published matrices plus synthetic layer-cake simulations, and the solver is sparse, so all of this runs in seconds on the 3060.
value: It finds and fixes the one wrong relation or mis-typed layer behind a contradiction, not just reporting that a cycle exists.

label: g1_loop
name: Linkage-Split Axe Signatures
mech: The task is attributing hand-hewn timber in historic buildings to individual axes and carpenters from phone photos of tool marks. AI has been absent because there are no labels, marks are worn, and it is a craft-history niche. A small CNN (about 15M parameters) turns each mark into binary "nick loci", the presence of blade-edge defects at positions along the edge, and these are clustered into blade prototypes stored in RAM. Within each prototype, pairwise linkage disequilibrium between loci is measured. One blade should give independent noise, so significant LD means two blades were mixed together. A split tested by mutual information then creates two prototypes. If the LD pattern is nested (one nick set is a subset of the other), the split is re-typed as a resharpening successor edge in a time-ordered blade lineage. The encoder trains contrastively on augmented crops, with re-clustering after each split.
value: It recovers how many tools were used, their sequence, and the build phases of an undocumented structure from cheap photos.

label: g1_loop
name: Difference-Map Field Drain Recovery
mech: The task is mapping lost 19th-century clay field drains under farmland from drone RGB and thermal images taken after rain. AI has been absent because no ground truth exists and the drains are invisible, so only slow GPR surveys have been used. A 20M-parameter U-Net predicts surface wetness from a current drain graph, using a fast non-differentiable Darcy flow solve on a 512² grid, and observed minus predicted gives the difference map. Ridges above 3σ insert drain segments by tracing along the ridge, troughs below −3σ delete segments, and each edit is kept only if R-free, the error on 5% of held-out pixels, improves. The U-Net is pretrained on simulated fields with random drain layouts, then fine-tuned self-consistently on real flights. Everything fits easily in 12 GB.
value: It turns one post-rain drone flight into a validated drain network with honest error bars, which a pixel segmenter cannot do without labels.

label: g1_mechneg
name: Weathered Contact Ledger
mech: Task: dry-stone walling, choosing the next stone from an irregular pile. AI is absent here because a wall's stability only shows over seasons, and no dataset or reliable simulator exists. Phone depth video of each placed stone is fused on the GPU into contact patches, and a fixed, untrained curvature hash turns each patch into a 64-bit code. A ledger in RAM stores integer counts for pairs of codes, and 32 GB holds tens of millions of them. Each weekly rescan adds one count to every contact pair whose stones have not moved and deletes pairs that shifted, so there is no target and no error, only survival. To place a stone, the system ranks the scanned pile by the summed survival counts of each stone's possible contacts against the gap, a hash sweep that takes seconds.
value: It learns stability from real walls surviving frost and time, which no same-budget simulator or labelled set can supply.

label: g1_mechneg
name: Crackle-Gated Grain Map
mech: Task: choosing hand-plane direction and depth on figured wood (curly or interlocked grain) without tear-out. AI is absent because the work is tactile, every board is different, and tear-out only appears after the cut. Phone macro video of the board is cut into tiles, and a fixed random projection turns each tile into 2048 sparse binary cells. A contact microphone on the plane sorts each stroke, with a fixed spectral threshold, into a smooth hiss or a crackle. A 2048×16 cell-to-direction link table is updated locally: links active during a smooth stroke are strengthened and those active during a crackle are inhibited, and no output is ever scored. Recall is one sparse product per tile, so a full map of safe directions for the board renders live.
value: It gives a safe-planing map for a board it has never seen, learned from the sound of the user's own strokes.

label: g1_mechneg
name: Breath-Locked Drone Swarm
mech: Task: live accompaniment of unmetered, ornamented solo singing such as sean-nós or Persian āvāz, where beat- and score-based systems fail because there is no meter. A GPU bank of 8192 phase oscillators with periods from 0.2 to 20 s is driven by the singer's breath and syllable onsets, picked up by a phone microphone. Each oscillator shifts its frequency by the sign of its phase lag to the input, splits when it locks onto two alternating periods, and dies after a long time unlocked. Drone swells and harp strikes fire when large locked groups pass phase zero together, and a ring buffer of past phrase phases lets recurring phrases lock in again at once. Nothing is trained offline, and it runs in milliseconds within a few hundred MB.
value: It accompanies free-rhythm singing by following the singer's breathing, which tempo trackers and sequence models cannot do on any budget.
